title: Segal homotopy categories and invariance of invertibility along arrow components
statement:
Use small simplicial sets, Kan complexes, components and weak homotopy equivalences from [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], the Kan model structure from [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], and Reedy fibrancy from [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure]. Let $W:\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{sSet}$ be Reedy fibrant, and suppose that each consecutive-edge map $W_n\to W_1\times_{W_0}\cdots\times_{W_0}W_1$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for $n\geq2$. For vertices $x,y\in W_0$, let $M_W(x,y)$ be the strict fiber of $(d_1,d_0):W_1\to W_0^2$. The objects $x\in(W_0)_0$, morphism sets $\pi_0M_W(x,y)$, identities represented by $s_0x$, and composition obtained by lifting two consecutive arrows to $W_2$ and applying $d_1$ form a well-defined unital associative category $hW$. Every map of such simplicial spaces induces a functor on these categories by its maps on objects and mapping spaces.

If vertices $g,g'\in W_1$ belong to the same path component of $W_1$, then the class of $g$ is an isomorphism in $hW$ if and only if the class of $g'$ is an isomorphism in $hW$, even when their source and target vertices differ. Consequently, if $W_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the union of components of $W_1$ that contain an isomorphism, then every vertex of $W_{\mathrm{eq}}$ represents an isomorphism, and its strict fiber at $(x,y)$ is precisely the union of the isomorphism components of $M_W(x,y)$.

source.place: Rezk, A model for the homotopy theory of homotopy theory, Sections 5.1-5.7, Proposition 5.4 and Lemma 5.8, printed pp. 11-14. Read online 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this Segal-space result.

proof.text: Use the representables $F(n)$ and the simplicial mapping spaces $\operatorname{Map}$ of [lem-coef-simplicial-space-reedy-cartesian]. Explicitly, evaluation on $(\mathrm{id}_{[n]},\mathrm{id}_{[q]})$ identifies $\operatorname{Map}(F(n),W)_q$ with $(W_n)_q$: given $w\in(W_n)_q$, the inverse sends $\alpha:[k]\to[n]$ and $\beta:[r]\to[q]$ to $\beta^*W(\alpha)(w)$. These formulas commute with both simplicial operators and are mutually inverse by naturality. The Reedy and Kan model statements make every $W_n$ Kan. The degree-one matching formula gives a Kan fibration $p=(d_1,d_0):W_1\to W_0^2$, so its strict fibers $M_W(x,y)$ are Kan: a horn-filling problem in a fiber is a lifting problem for $p$ with constant lower simplex. More generally, for any inclusion $A\subseteq B$ of simplicial spaces, the mapping-space fibration clause applied to $W\to *$ makes restriction $\operatorname{Map}(B,W)\to\operatorname{Map}(A,W)$ a Kan fibration. Let $G(n)\subseteq F(n)$ be the union of the consecutive edges. A map from $G(n)$ is exactly a list of $n$ arrows agreeing at successive endpoints, so restriction is the assumed Segal map $\phi_n:W_n\to W_1\times_{W_0}\cdots\times_{W_0}W_1$. It is a fibration and a weak equivalence, hence a trivial fibration. Restricting to fixed vertices $(x_0,\ldots,x_n)$ is a pullback and still has the right lifting property against all boundaries: compose a proposed lifting square with the pullback projections, lift there, and use the fixed-vertex equation to land back in the pullback. Denote this restriction by $\phi_{n,\mathbf x}:W_n(\mathbf x)\to\prod_{i=1}^nM_W(x_{i-1},x_i)$.

source.place: Rezk §§2.5, 4.1 and 5.1, printed pp. 7, 11–12; trivial fibrations on fixed-vertex fibers spelled out.

proof.text: The component-comparison statement identifies $\pi_0$ of every Kan mapping fiber with vertices modulo finite edge chains, so all morphism classes have vertex representatives. For arrows $f:x\to y$ and $g:y\to z$, lift $(f,g)$ through $\phi_{2,(x,y,z)}$ and define their composite class by applying $d_1$. Boundary lifting in dimension zero supplies a lift. Boundary lifting in dimension one, with both endpoints prescribed and constant image $(f,g)$, joins any two lifts, so their middle faces give the same component of $M_W(x,z)$. If a representative $f$ or $g$ changes along one edge in its fixed-endpoint mapping fiber, horn lifting in dimension one lifts the resulting edge of pairs starting at a chosen lift; its middle face joins the composite representatives. Apply this to finite edge chains to see that composition depends only on the input components. For three arrows $f:x_0\to x_1$, $g:x_1\to x_2$, $h:x_2\to x_3$, lift $(f,g,h)$ to $T\in W_3(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3)$. Its faces $d_3T,d_1T$ represent $g\circ f$ followed by $h$, and $d_0T,d_2T$ represent $f$ followed by $h\circ g$. Their final middle faces agree because $d_1d_1T=d_1d_2T$. Independence of lifts just proved gives associativity for arbitrary choices. The degenerate triangles $s_0f$ and $s_1f$ have consecutive edges $(s_0x,f)$ and $(f,s_0y)$ and middle face $f$, giving both unit laws. Thus the claimed category $hW$ is well defined.

source.place: Rezk §5.3 and Proposition 5.4, printed pp. 12–13; representative independence expanded by boundary and horn lifting.

proof.text: A map $W\to W'$ sends a strict mapping fiber at $(x,y)$ to the strict mapping fiber at the image pair, and hence sends edge chains to edge chains. It sends a triangle lifting a pair to a triangle lifting its image pair, and commutes with its middle face; thus it preserves the composite classes of Step 2. It commutes with $s_0$, so preserves identities as well. These maps on vertices and on morphism classes give the asserted functor.

source.place: Rezk §5.5, printed p. 13; naturality of the explicit triangle construction.

proof.text: We prove the inverse-witness criterion needed for transport, rather than assume it. Inside $F(3)$ let $Z$ be the union of edges $02$, $12$, $13$ and their vertices; it is the discrete nerve of $0\to2\leftarrow1\to3$. The restriction $r:W_3\to\operatorname{Map}(Z,W)$ is a Kan fibration by the mapping-space statement, since $Z\hookrightarrow F(3)$ is a monomorphism and $W\to *$ is Reedy fibrant. Order its three arrow coordinates as $(13,12,02)$. For $g:x\to y$, let $t(g)$ have vertices $(y,x,y,x)$ and these coordinates $(s_0x,g,s_0y)$. If $H$ lifts $t(g)$, its edges $a=01:y\to x$ and $b=23:y\to x$, together with its triangular faces, give $[g][a]=1_y$ and $[b][g]=1_x$ in $hW$. Associativity gives $[b]=[b]([g][a])=([b][g])[a]=[a]$, so $[g]$ is invertible. Conversely suppose $[g]$ is invertible, choose a representative $h:y\to x$ of its inverse and lift the spine $(h,g,h)$ to $T\in W_3(y,x,y,x)$. Then $r(T)$ has middle coordinate $g$; coordinates $13$ and $02$ represent $[h][g]=1_x$ and $[g][h]=1_y$. They can therefore be joined to $s_0x$ and $s_0y$ by finite edge chains inside $M_W(x,x)$ and $M_W(y,y)$. Vary one such coordinate at a time, holding $g$ and all four vertices fixed, to obtain an edge chain in $\operatorname{Map}(Z,W)$ from $r(T)$ to $t(g)$. Lift each edge through the Kan fibration $r$, starting at the already chosen endpoint; lifting is available with either endpoint prescribed, by the two one-dimensional horns. The final vertex is a lift of $t(g)$. This proves both directions of the criterion.

source.place: Rezk §5.5, printed p. 13, zigzag-lift characterization; its omitted converse is supplied explicitly.

proof.text: For an edge $G:\Delta^1\to W_1$, the degeneracies of its two endpoint paths and $G$ itself give a path $t(G)$ in $\operatorname{Map}(Z,W)$, with the four object paths ordered as $(d_0G,d_1G,d_0G,d_1G)$ and arrow coordinates $(s_0d_1G,G,s_0d_0G)$. If either endpoint arrow represents an isomorphism, Step 4 supplies a lift of $t(G)$ at that endpoint. Lift this path through $r$ using the one-dimensional horn at that endpoint. Its other endpoint is a lift of $t$ of the other arrow, which is therefore invertible by Step 4. The component comparison in [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre], applied to the Kan complex $W_1$, says that membership of vertices in one realized path component is exactly the equivalence relation generated by edges. Iterating the preceding lifting argument over that finite edge chain proves the equivalence of invertibility for $g$ and $g'$. No endpoints are held fixed here; the explicit four object paths are why the argument permits sources and targets to vary.

source.place: Rezk Lemma 5.8, printed p. 13; finite edge-chain reduction and moving-object coordinates made explicit.

proof.text: For any simplicial set the simplices whose vertices lie in a chosen union of edge components form a simplicial subset: all vertices of a simplex are joined by its edges, and faces and degeneracies preserve their component. Apply this to define $W_{\mathrm{eq}}\subseteq W_1$. Step 5 says every vertex of this subset represents an isomorphism. A vertex of the strict fiber at $(x,y)$ lies in $W_{\mathrm{eq}}$ exactly when its arrow represents an isomorphism in $hW$. Along any edge of $M_W(x,y)$ the morphism component, and hence this property, is constant. Thus precisely the mapping-fiber components representing isomorphisms occur. At every higher simplicial degree membership is likewise determined by the vertices, so this identifies the strict fiber as a simplicial subset, not merely its vertex set.

source.place: Rezk §5.7 and the pullback square (6.3), printed pp. 13–14; simplicial-subset identification expanded.
